list.listitem: Endoscopy is the preferred method of diagnosis for a Mallory-Weiss tear (MWT). B

Although most MWTs will heal spontaneously, treatment may be required on the basis of severity or persistence of bleeding; endoscopic intervention with multipolar electrocautery, epinephrine injection, band ligation, or clips are all similarly effective options. B
Refeeding may occur immediately after stabilization in non-rebleeding tears. B
Risk factors for recurrent bleeding or complications include shock or low hematocrit on initial presentation, coagulopathy, and active bleeding on endoscopy. B

background.definition: MWT is characterized by upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding secondary to lacerations of the mucosa of the distal esophagus, gastroesophageal junction or gastric cardia. It is usually associated with persistent retching or any event that causes a sudden rise in intragastric pressure.

list.listitem: MWT accounts for 5% to 7% of upper GI bleeds.
MWT is more common in men than women (approximately 2:1 to 4:1 ratio). There is no racial predilection.
Age range is wide, although majority present in 40s or 50s.
MWT risk factors are alcohol use, alcohol binge, cyclical vomiting, bulimia nervosa and NSAID use.. Literature is conflicted on whether MWT is associated with hiatal hernia
A large, transient, rapidly occurring pressure gradient across the gastroesophageal junction can cause the tear.
Another cause is acute dilation of the nondistensible lower esophagus, producing a linear tear in the mucosa.
Rarely, MWT can be caused by endoscopy.
Rapid rise of intragastric pressure causes longitudinal lacerations across the lesser curvature of the gastric cardia or lower esophagus.
Violent prolapse of the upper stomach into the esophagus across a hiatal hernia is a second potential mechanism.
The lesser curvature of stomach and the right lateral esophageal wall are the areas that are commonly affected because muscle thickness is usually thin in these areas.
The classic description is a history of vomiting or retching followed by hematemesis, but only 30% of patients have this presentation. C
Risk factors and historical clues to MWT include alcoholic binge drinking; protracted or violent retching or vomiting; and other causes of acute, intense increased gastric pressure. C
Endoscopy is the preferred method of diagnosis and can identify the cause of upper GI bleeding 95% of the time. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Associated with Helicobacter pylori, NSAID use; dyspepsia, previous ulcer disease; improved with food
Intermittent bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, older age, painless
Associated with severe gastroesophageal reflux disease; hematemesis
Early satiety, indigestion, melena, hematemesis, older age, weight loss; history of smoking, alcohol consumption

list.listitem: The classic presentation is a history of vomiting or retching followed by hematemesis, but only 30% of patients with MWT present this way.

Up to 50% of patients have hematemesis on first emesis. Less common presentations are abdominal pain, hematochezia, melena, and syncope. Other precipitating factors include alcohol binging, straining, lifting, coughing, and severe gastric blunt trauma.
There are no typical physical findings for MWT, but signs will relate to degree of GI blood loss and may include tachycardia, hypotension, orthostatic, or frank shock.
The Glasgow-Blatchford Score may be used to identify patients who may be considered for discharge and outpatient endoscopy. A score of 0-1 is low risk and >1 i s considered high risk

Endoscopy should be the initial method to identify and treat acute upper GI bleeding. Endoscopy identifies the source in 95% of cases, and it can help to establish the risk of rebleeding and mortality.
Endoscopic diagnosis usually based on adherent clot, active bleeding at site of laceration, or fibrin crust over a mucosal tear. Most patients have stopped bleeding at time of endoscopy.
The most common finding is a small (2-3 cm) linear tear or tears below the gastroesophageal junction on the lesser curvature.
Mucosal lesions that predispose to bleeding (esophagitis, ulcers) may be associated with MWT.

Obtain a hemoglobin and hematocrit to assess initial severity and then subsequently to monitor patients. Obtain a platelet count, prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, or coagulation studies to identify coagulopathy.
Order electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, coagulation studies- PT/INR and creatinine. Also order blood type and antibody screening for patients who require transfusions.
Barium or Gastrografin studies are not recommended; they are not sensitive for this diagnosis and will interfere with endoscopy.
Consider high dose PPI prior to endoscopy
Patients with an upper GI bleed who are suspected of MWT by history of recurrent vomiting should be assessed for hemodynamic stability and continued bleeding.
Unstable patients should be hospitalized and monitored with emergent endoscopy. Stable patients may be managed as outpatients with endoscopy to be done within 24 hours.
Laboratory studies for outpatients should include hemoglobin, hematocrit, and coagulation studies. Inpatients should have additional testing based on circumstance (see "Diagnostic testing").
Transfuse red blood cells RBC to hemodynamically stable patients with hemoglobin ≤ 7. For patients with cardiovascular disease, example Coronary artery disease, ≤ 8 should prompy transfusion.

For patients on antiocagulants or antiplatelets; --Withhold direct acting anticoagulants (DOACs) --Do not withhold low dose aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention and if held restart as soon as possible.--Consider reveral of DOAC and vitamin K antagonist in patients with hemodynamic instability
Most episodes will resolve spontaneously; adherent clot or nonbleeding visible vessels are usually not treated unless there is a coagulopathy. B

If the MWT does not spontaneously resolve or if bleeding is clinically significant, endoscopic intervention with endoscopic band ligation or endoscopic through-the-scope clip over epinephrine injection alone.B
Refeeding may occur immediately after stabilization in non-rebleeding MWT. B
Routine second look endoscopy is not recommended but may be considered in patients who are at high risk for rebleeding
Although uncommon, in patients with copious hematemesis and at risk of airway compromise perform endotracheal intubation.

Acid-suppression therapy, usually a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole, H2 antagonist such as ranitidine, and mucosal protectant such as sucralfate, are prescribed for 1 to 2 weeks to accelerate healing, although evidence from clinical trials to support this practice is lacking.
Antiemetic drugs may be helpful to control nausea and vomiting.
Resume initially held anticoagulants after hemostasis is secured.
Most patients will resolve spontaneously; only 5% to 35% will require therapeutic intervention. Adherent clot or nonbleeding visible vessels are usually not treated unless there is a coagulopathy.
Endoscopically guided multipolar electrocoagulation, epinephrine injection, band ligation, or clips are all treatment options.

In patients with active bleeding from MWTs (oozing and spurting), a Canadian guideline (2025) suggests endoscopic band ligation or endoscopic through-the-scope clip over epinephrine injection alone. The guideline advises against endoscopic hemostatic therapy for nonbleeding MWTs with visible vessels, adherent clots, flat pigmented spots, or clean-based ulcers.

Five small controlled trials of endoscopic treatment of MWT treatment were identified. A comparison of clips with epinephrine injection in 35 patients found no difference in outcomes, as did a comparison of band ligation with epinephrine injection in 34 patients, a comparison of band ligation with clip placement in 41 patients, and a nonrandomized comparison of band ligation with electrocautery in 58 patients. A comparison of epinephrine injection with no endoscopic therapy found improved outcomes with treatment, and a case series of band ligation reported good outcomes.
Epinephrine injection should be used with caution in significant cardiovascular disease.

Angiotherapy with vasopressin infusion and gastric artery embolization are reserved for those who either fail or are at high risk for endoscopic complications. Surgical oversewing of the tear is rarely required, and then only in cases refractory to other endoscopic treatments.
Endoscopic band ligation may be especially helpful in cases of concomitant portal hypertension or varices.
Endoscopic hemoclipping approximates the margins of the tear and causes less tissue injury than thermal methods.
Balloon tamponade should be avoided as it reproduces the causative factors of MWT.
Sclerosants (alcohol and polidocanol) are an option but may cause tissue necrosis and increase risk of perforation.
Fasting is recommended only for unstable patients or for duration of time prior to endoscopy.
Food intake may resume after endoscopy and advance as tolerated over 48 hours.

Actively bleeding MWT and hemodynamically unstable patients should be hospitalized and observed for 48 hours for rebleeding, especially if initial episode was significant or there are endoscopic findings of clot, visible vessel, or hyperpigmented protuberance.
Rebleeding is most likely to occur within this 48-hour period.

Inpatient care depends on magnitude of the bleed. Monitor vital signs, serial hemoglobin, and hematocrit; hemodynamically support patient if necessary with transfusion as indicated for severe bleeding.
Prognosis is generally good. Most patients stop bleeding spontaneously, and MWTs usually heal within 48 to 72 hours. B
Routine second look endoscopy is not recommended.
Patients with low hematocrit upon hospital admission are at greatest risk for complications, even if there are no antecedent risk factors. B
Other risk factors include active bleeding, coagulopathy, and shock on presentation. B
Pregnancy-related MWT may be very minimal, self-limiting, and recurrent. Small drops of blood with morning sickness-related emesis may not require endoscopy.
If bleeding is significant, endoscopy may be performed; several small trials have shown no fetal- or pregnancy-related adverse effects.
Sucralfate is pregnancy class B, whereas proton pump inhibitors and antiemetics such as Compazine are pregnancy class C (safety in pregnancy has not been established).
Sucralfate has been used at 40 to 80 mg/kg every 6 hours, but safety is not established.
Safety of PPI has not been established in children.
Compazine may be used by oral or rectal route.
